verses.text: When the kingdom of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned Yahweh’s law, and all Israel with him.
In the fifth year of king Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, because they had trespassed against Yahweh,
with twelve hundred chariots, and sixty thousand horsemen. The people were without number who came with him out of Egypt: the Lubim, the Sukkiim, and the Ethiopians.
He took the fortified cities which belonged to Judah, and came to Jerusalem.

Now Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam, and to the princes of Judah, who were gathered together to Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, “Yahweh says, ‘You have forsaken me, therefore I have also left you in the hand of Shishak.’”
Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves; and they said, “Yahweh is righteous.”

When Yahweh saw that they humbled themselves, Yahweh’s word came to Shemaiah, saying, “They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them; but I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath won’t be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.
Nevertheless they will be his servants, that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.”

So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of Yahweh’s house and the treasures of the king’s house. He took it all away. He also took away the shields of gold which Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place, and committed them to the hands of the captains of the guard, who kept the door of the king’s house.
As often as the king entered into Yahweh’s house, the guard came and bore them, then brought them back into the guard room.
When he humbled himself, Yahweh’s wrath turned from him, so as not to destroy him altogether. Moreover, there were good things found in Judah.

So king Rehoboam strengthened himself in Jerusalem and reigned; for Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which Yahweh had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess.
He did that which was evil, because he didn’t set his heart to seek Yahweh.

Now the acts of Rehoboam, first and last, aren’t they written in the histories of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, in the genealogies? There were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.
Rehoboam slept with his fathers, and was buried in David’s city; and Abijah his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: Rehoboam's strength becomes his peril. We often see it in life—the moment we feel secure, we turn from the One who gives that security. Solomon's kingdom was strong, and so was Rehoboam's, but strength without faithfulness becomes a kind of blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shishak of Egypt—a real king whose invasion is written on temple walls still standing. When we turn from the Lord, history turns against us. The fifth year marks how quickly abundance can become judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen—numbers meant to crush hope. Yet the chronicler names them not to glorify them, but to show how small they make human pride. The 'people without number' serve as a mirror of judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fortified cities fall first; Jerusalem waits. Each conquest is a step closer to the heart of the kingdom. Sometimes the Lord allows our outer defenses to crumble to teach us where real safety lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shemaiah the prophet speaks the hard word: 'You have forsaken me, therefore I have also left you.' The Lord's silence is often His clearest message—a mercy that lets us feel the consequence of our choices.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In one verse, Rehoboam and his princes move from folly to humility. There is grace in this turning—not because they deserve it, but because the Lord's mercy meets us the instant we break before Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh saw their humbling and relented. Not completely—Shishak will still take the treasures—but enough to save them from destruction. Sometimes mercy means we are spared the final blow, not freed from all consequence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'They will be his servants, that they may know my service.' Captivity to a foreign king becomes a school. The Lord often humbles us into learning what we would not choose to know—His faithfulness, His reign, His mercy toward the broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's gold shields are taken. The treasures of the temple are plundered. Yet notice: the Lord Himself is not taken. His presence remains, though His people have stripped the house bare by their unfaithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam replaces the gold shields with brass. A practical act, yes, but also a picture: when our treasures are stripped, we learn to build with lesser things. The replacement guards Jerusalem still—not with splendor, but with faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each time the king enters the temple, the guards carry the brass shields and return them to the guard room. A small ritual of humility, repeated. The Lord often teaches us not through grand moments but through small, faithful repetitions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Rehoboam humbled himself, the Lord's wrath turned. Readers today hear an echo in their own reversals—the moment we stop resisting grace and instead surrender, we find the anger of a Father turns to protection. His wrath departs; good things return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam was forty-one when he began to reign, and ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem—the city Yahweh had chosen. Even a broken king sits in a chosen place. The kingdom's weakness does not change its vocation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did evil, because he didn't set his heart to seek Yahweh. Not weakness, but unwillingness. The chronicler names the root: a heart that chose not to seek. This is the plain center of all our falling away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His acts are written in 'the histories of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer.' A subtle grace: his deeds are recorded not by historians alone, but by those who spoke for God. Even a failed king remains under the chronicling of prophecy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam slept with his fathers in David's city. His reign ended; Abijah followed. This is how the chronicles speak: not with judgment, but with the simple rhythm of succession. Kings come and go, but the kingdom endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
